    # start time is 9:00 AM.
    base_hour = 9
    hour = base_hour + mins // 60
    minute = mins % 60
    period = "AM"
    if hour >= 12:
        period = "PM"
        if hour > 12:
            hour = hour - 12
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{period}"

# Define the travel time matrix (in minutes)
travel_times = {
    "Haight-Ashbury": {"Fisherman's Wharf": 23, "Richmond District": 10, "Mission District": 11, "Bayview": 18},
    "Fisherman's Wharf": {"Haight-Ashbury": 22, "Richmond District": 18, "Mission District": 22, "Bayview": 26},
    "Richmond District": {"Haight-Ashbury": 10, "Fisherman's Wharf": 18, "Mission District": 20, "Bayview": 26},
    "Mission District": {"Haight-Ashbury": 12, "Fisherman's Wharf": 22, "Richmond District": 20, "Bayview": 15},
    "Bayview": {"Haight-Ashbury": 19, "Fisherman's Wharf": 25, "Richmond District": 25, "Mission District": 13}
}

# Define friends along with their meeting info.
# Times are in minutes after 9:00AM.
friends = [
    {
        "name": "Mary",
        "location": "Richmond District",
        "available_start": 240,   # 1:00PM
        "available_end": 615,     # 7:15PM (9:00AM + 10h15 = 615)
        "duration": 75
    },
    {
        "name": "Sarah",
        "location": "Fisherman's Wharf",
        "available_start": 345,   # 2:45PM
        "available_end": 510,     # 5:30PM
        "duration": 105
    },

        "name": "Helen",
        "location": "Mission District",
        "available_start": 765,   # 9:45PM
        "available_end": 810,     # 10:30PM
        "duration": 30
    },
    {
        "name": "Thomas",
        "location": "Bayview",
        "available_start": 375,   # 3:15PM
        "available_end": 585,     # 6:45PM
        "duration": 120
    }
]

# Simulate a given order of visits.
def simulate_itinerary(order):
    # itinerary will be a list of text steps.
    steps = []
    current_time = 0    # in minutes (9:00AM)
    current_loc = "Haight-Ashbury"
    steps.append(f'You start at {current_loc} at {minutes_to_time(current_time)}.')

    for friend in order:
        # Travel from current_loc to friend's location.
        travel_time = travel_times[current_loc][friend["location"]]
        departure_time = current_time
        arrival_time = departure_time + travel_time
        steps.append(
            f'You travel from {current_loc} to {friend["location"]} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival_time)}.'
        )
        # Wait if arrived earlier than friend's available start.
        meeting_start = max(arrival_time, friend["available_start"])
        if meeting_start > arrival_time:
            steps.append(f'You wait until {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)}.')
        meeting_end = meeting_start + friend["duration"]
        # Check feasibility: meeting must finish before friend’s available_end.
        if meeting_end > friend["available_end"]:
            return None  # Infeasible itinerary.
        steps.append(
            f'You meet {friend["name"]} for {friend["duration"]} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meeting_end)}.'
        )
        current_time = meeting_end
        current_loc = friend["location"]
    return steps, current_time

# We want to try itineraries that visit a subset of friends in some order.
# Our objective is to maximize the number of friends met.
best_itinerary = None
max_meetings = 0

for r in range(1, len(friends)+1):

def minutes_to_time(total_minutes):
    """
    Convert minutes elapsed from 9:00AM into a 12-hour time string.
    For example, 0 -> 9:00AM, 73 -> 10:13AM, 240 -> 1:00PM, etc.
    """
    # starting point is 9:00AM
    base_hour = 9
    hour = base_hour + total_minutes // 60
    minute = total_minutes % 60
    # Determine AM or PM (assume hours < 12 are AM, hours >= 12 are PM)
    # However, note that 9:00AM to, say, 22:30 is on the same day.
    period = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
    # Convert hour to 12-hour format:
    display_hour = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
    # Special case: if hour==12, then it remains 12.
    return f"{display_hour}:{minute:02d}{period}"

 • an “availability window” (the friend’s start–and–end times),
 • and the “distances” between their meeting locations (here, expressed in minutes).

 2. If you arrive before the friend’s start time, you wait until the friend’s available time begins. Your meeting then starts at the maximum of these two times.
 3. Check if the meeting (starting then and lasting the required minutes) can be completed before the friend’s end time.
 4. If yes, you record the travel step (and waiting, if needed) and then the meeting step. Your “current time” is updated to the end of the meeting and your “current location” to the friend’s district.
Then you “branch” and try to schedule a next friend (from the ones you have not yet visited). In a depth–first search you keep track of the best (largest count) overall schedule.

We can “model” this problem as a time‐window routing/scheduling problem. In our case we start at Haight-Ashbury at 9:00AM (i.e. 540 minutes after midnight) and we have nine friends located in different districts. Each friend has a time window during which they’re available as well as a minimum meeting duration. In addition, travel between locations takes a known number of minutes (and note that travel times are not completely symmetric). Our goal is to plan a route (i.e. an ordering of friends) and schedule meeting start times (including waiting if we arrive early) so that for each friend we:
  • depart from our current location at a known time,
  • add the travel time to reach the next friend’s district,
  • begin the meeting at the later of our arrival time or the friend’s available‐start time,
  • ensure that starting the meeting that late still leaves enough time to complete the required minimum duration before the friend’s closing time.
Our “simulation” therefore works as follows:
 1. Start with the current location (“Haight-Ashbury”) at 9:00AM.
 2. For a given friend (with a known district, available window [available_start, available_end] and meeting duration), determine the arrival time:
  – arrival_time = current_time + travel_time(current_location, friend_location).
 3. The meeting cannot start before the friend’s available_start so set:
  – meeting_start = max(arrival_time, available_start).
 4. Check feasibility by making sure that meeting_start is not too late (i.e. meeting_start must be ≤ available_end – meeting_duration).

General Reasoning and Approach:

1. Represent each “meeting‐stop” (each friend) as an object with:
  – a name,

  – and a minimum meeting duration.

  a. The travel time from our current location.
  b. The arrival time = current time + travel.
  c. The meeting can only begin at the later of our arrival and the friend’s available‐start.

4. Our goal is to maximize the number of friends met without breaking any time–window or duration constraint. This is similar to a “vehicle routing with time windows” or “orienteering” problem. best_count = 0

def dfs(current_location, current_time, visited, schedule):
    global best_schedule, best_count
    progressed = False
    
    # Try each friend not yet visited.
    for friend in friends:
        if friend["name"] in visited:
            continue
        
        # Get travel time from current location to friend's location.
        travel = travel_times[current_location][friend["location"]]
        arrival_time = current_time + travel
        
        # The meeting may only begin after the friend becomes available.
        meeting_start = arrival_time if arrival_time >= friend["avail_start"] else friend["avail_start"]
        meeting_end = meeting_start + friend["duration"]
        
        # Check feasibility: meeting must end before the friend’s availability ends.
        if meeting_end > friend["avail_end"]:
            continue  # not possible to meet this friend given our schedule
        
        # Build the narrative steps for moving from current location to meeting friend.
        new_schedule = deepcopy(schedule)
        travel_step = f"You travel to {friend['location']} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival_time)}."
        new_schedule.append(travel_step)
        
        if arrival_time < friend["avail_start"]:
            wait_step = f"You wait until {format_time(friend['avail_start'])}."
            new_schedule.append(wait_step)
        
        meeting_step = (f"You meet {friend['name']} for {friend['duration']} minutes "
                        f"from {format_time(meeting_start)} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
        new_schedule.append(meeting_step)
        
        # Recurse: mark this friend as visited.
        new_visited = visited.union({friend["name"]})
        dfs(friend["location"], meeting_end, new_visited, new_schedule)
        progressed = True
    
    # If no further friend can be added then update best schedule if current one is better.
    if not progressed:
        if len(visited) > best_count:
            best_count = len(visited)
            best_schedule = schedule

    # This helper converts it to an "H:MMAM/PM" string.
    hour = minutes // 60

    if hour >= 12:

    if hour == 0:

    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{period}"

def dfs(current_time, current_location, visited, itinerary):
    global best_schedule, best_count
    # Update the best solution if the current one is better (by count of friends met)
    if len(visited) > best_count:
        best_count = len(visited)
        best_schedule = itinerary[:]
    
    # For every friend not yet visited, try schedule a meeting if possible.
    for friend_name, info in friends.items():
        if friend_name in visited:

        # Get travel time from current location to friend location.
        if current_location not in travel_times or info["location"] not in travel_times[current_location]:
            continue  # no travel info so skip
        travel = travel_times[current_location][info["location"]]
        arrival_time = current_time + travel
        # The meeting can start no earlier than the friend’s available start.
        meeting_start = max(arrival_time, info["window_start"])
        # Check if we can finish the meeting before the friend leaves.
        if meeting_start + info["duration"] > info["window_end"]:
            continue  # Not enough time to meet this friend.
        
        # Prepare new steps for the itinerary.
        new_itinerary = itinerary[:]
        travel_step = (f"You travel from {current_location} to {info['location']} in {travel} minutes "
                        f"and arrive at {convert_time(arrival_time)}.")
        new_itinerary.append(travel_step)
        if meeting_start > arrival_time:
            wait_step = f"You wait until {convert_time(meeting_start)}."
            new_itinerary.append(wait_step)
        meeting_end = meeting_start + info["duration"]
        meet_step = (f"You meet {friend_name} for {info['duration']} minutes from "
                     f"{convert_time(meeting_start)} to {convert_time(meeting_end)}.")
        new_itinerary.append(meet_step)

We can think of the “friends‐meeting” problem as a time–window scheduling (or “orienteering”) problem where you must decide the order in which to “serve” (meet) friends while respecting not only the travel times between “nodes” (each friend’s location) but also each friend’s time‐window and minimum meeting duration. One way to solve such a problem is to “fix” any segments that are forced by the constraints and then use a search (for example, via depth‐first “backtracking”) over the remaining visits. In our case the morning is nearly forced:
 • You start at The Castro at 9:00AM.
 • You immediately travel to Presidio (20 minutes) so that you can meet Joshua (who is available from 8:30AM to 1:15PM) for a contiguous 105 minutes.
 • Then you travel from Presidio to Embarcadero (20 minutes) and meet David (available 10:45–12:30) for 30 minutes.
 • Then you travel from Embarcadero to Alamo Square (19 minutes) arriving very early—but Stephanie only is available from 3:30–4:30PM, so you must wait until 3:30PM for that meeting.

Once “evening” begins we have a choice among six friends (the ones with later availabilities at Financial District, Haight-Ashbury, Golden Gate Park, Sunset District, Marina District, and North Beach). (Ronald is not feasible because his window [8:00–9:30AM] would require you to be there before your start time at Castro; and Elizabeth’s window, for example, nearly “uses up” its time‐window so that it often conflicts with Timothy’s later availability.) One can then “simulate” every possible order (or use dynamic programming) in which, starting from your current state (at Alamo Square after you meet Stephanie) you try to “chain” visits so that for each candidate friend you:
 1. Compute the travel time from your current location;
 2. Determine the earliest arrival time and the earliest possible meeting start (which is the later of your arrival and the friend’s available–start time);
 3. Check that you can “fit in” the friend’s required meeting duration (i.e. that meeting start plus the required “service time” does not exceed the friend’s available–end time).

Our code therefore “hard–codes” the morning appointments (Joshua and David must be met, and then you wait and meet Stephanie at Alamo Square) and then uses DFS (depth–first search) for the “evening” portion. In our “manual” exploration an optimal chain was found (one example) which is:
 Stephanie (at Alamo Square, 3:30–4:00PM) →
 Kimberly (at Haight‑Ashbury; travel “Alamo–to–Haight”: 5 minutes, wait until her window opens at 4:45PM, meet for 75 minutes until 6:00PM) →

 Timothy (at North Beach; travel 23 minutes arriving at about 7:15PM, then wait until his 7:45PM start and meet for 90 minutes until 9:15PM).

Thus overall you are “on–time” for Joshua and David in the morning and then meet four friends in the evening for a total of six friends met.

Each friend is available at a certain location during a given time window and you must “serve” them for a minimum meeting duration. In addition, when you travel between locations the travel–time (which is not symmetric in general) must be added and if you arrive early you wait until the friend’s window starts. In other words, if you are at your current location at time T and want to “serve” friend X (with location Lx, available from t_start to t_end and meeting duration d), then you:
 • compute the travel time (say t_travel) from your current location to Lx,
 • set your arrival time = T + t_travel,
 • if you arrive before t_start, then you wait until t_start;
 • start the meeting at max(arrival time, t_start) and finish d minutes later;
 • accept friend X only if the meeting finish time is not later than t_end.
Your goal is to choose the order in which you “serve” friends so that the number of friends met is maximized.

One general solution method is to use a depth–first search (or branch–and–bound) where the state is (current location, current time, set of friends already met, and the schedule so far). For each remaining friend you try to “branch” if the travel plus meeting can be completed before the friend’s window ends.  • add the travel time,
 • potentially wait if you arrive before the friend’s window opens, and then
 • schedule a meeting that lasts the required minimum time without “running past” that friend’s end time.

A general solution method is:
